name: Sture
title: Sture Tanker Gauging | UTM at Oseberg Crude Terminal, Norway
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Sture on the Hjeltefjord: crude export tankers at the terminal, ballast tanks, deck and piping gauged within permit rules.
h1: Thickness Gauging for Crude Tankers Loading at Sture, Norway
intro: Sture is a crude oil export terminal on the Hjeltefjord north of Bergen, built around rock-cavern storage that is fed by pipeline from the Oseberg area. Tankers arrive, load and leave, and the terminal sets the pace. Gauging here means well-chosen spaces and careful permits. Atlantis sends technicians from India to join the tanker at the jetty, read ballast spaces, deck and piping, and report in the class formats.

highlights.h: Crude export tankers at one jetty
highlights.p: The terminal loads crude for export, so ship types are narrow: mostly medium and large crude carriers. That lets us prepare a standard ballast-side scope in advance and adapt it to each ship's age and class record.

highlights.h: Permit-led work at a hazardous site
highlights.p: Nothing happens at the jetty without a permit. We submit team details early, bring equipment suited to the zone, and plan the scope so that ballast spaces, deck and piping are read while cargo operations proceed.

Crude tankers face Enhanced Survey Programme thickness measurement at renewal. Readings taken here show how wastage is developing, so the owner can plan steel renewal and the yard can prepare materials.

port.h: Sture: a rock-cavern crude terminal on the Hjeltefjord
p: Sture lies on the Hjeltefjord, the sheltered deep fjord that runs north to south between the islands west of Bergen and the mainland. Ships approach from the open North Sea through the fairways monitored by vessel traffic services at Fedje, then follow the fjord to the jetties. The terminal receives crude oil by pipeline and stores it in caverns blasted out of the rock, ready to be loaded onto export tankers. The site is industrial and compact, set in a fjord landscape of steep shores, and the water is deep enough close to the jetties for large tankers.

The traffic is therefore predictable in kind if not in timing. Crude oil export tankers, from medium-sized vessels to larger crude carriers, arrive to load cargo for refineries in Europe and beyond, and tugs, mooring launches and pilot boats support each call. Calls last as long as it takes to load the cargo and complete the paperwork, and the ship then sails. Weather rarely stops operations inside the fjord, though strong winds and poor visibility can delay arrivals and departures, so cargo programmes are scheduled with slack.

From a gauging view, a tanker at Sture is often arriving on ballast, with ballast tanks that have been in service for the voyage, and leaving full of crude. That sequence suits ballast-side work: segregated ballast tanks, forepeak and cofferdams can be gauged while the ship is alongside, with cargo operations proceeding elsewhere. The same applies to deck plating and external pipe runs outside the hazardous zone. Cargo-tank readings are usually left for drydock or for a period when the ship is gas-free, because loading, hazard zones and terminal rules restrict what can be done at the jetty.

facilities.h: Where a tanker can be gauged at Sture
p: The jetty is the main location. The tanker's agent submits the team's names and equipment list well ahead of the call, the terminal issues passes and safety instruction, and the master and terminal agree a permit to work before boarding. Our instruments and couplants are chosen to suit the hazardous-area rules, and the scope is divided between spaces that can be read while cargo moves and spaces that must wait. Ballast tanks need to be ventilated and gas-free in advance, so the crew starts preparation on passage to the terminal.

There is no repair yard at Sture, and ships that need steel renewal usually dock at yards on the Norwegian coast or elsewhere in northern Europe. Gauging at the jetty gives the steel estimate and a record that class and the yard can use in planning. Tankers sometimes wait in sheltered fjord waters for a berth, and a short launch-borne scope on deck and in accessible tanks may be possible there, though the terminal's rules and the weather decide.
list: Terminal jetties: deck plating, external piping and manifold-area structure outside the cargo hazard zone.
Segregated ballast tanks: wing, double-bottom and peak tanks entered under permit once gas-free.
Forepeak, aft peak and cofferdams: readings taken while loading continues in the cargo tanks.
Engine room and sea-water piping: scrubber overboard lines and cooling systems on tankers fitted with scrubbers.
Fjord anchorage areas: short launch-borne scopes on tankers waiting for the berth, subject to terminal rules.

context.h: Norwegian port state control, vetting and the tanker trade
p: Norway is a Paris MoU member, and port state control is carried out by the Norwegian Maritime Authority. Crude oil tankers are among the ship types that inspectors look at most closely, especially older vessels, where structural condition in ballast spaces and the deck is examined and thickness records may be requested. Norway is also part of the European Economic Area, so many EU maritime rules, including those on hazardous materials inventories for ships, apply through the EEA Agreement.

Tanker vetting is a commercial discipline here. Terminal operators and charterers inspect crude tankers against industry vetting standards, and a vessel with documented wastage close to the allowable diminution and no repair plan will draw questions. An owner trading medium and large crude tankers from the Norwegian terminals therefore benefits from current thickness evidence. Since the terminal is in a sensitive fjord environment, environmental rules add care around any leak or spill risk, which is another reason to keep piping and deck steel in sound condition.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Sture
jobs.p: Jobs at Sture are limited by the terminal rules and cargo status, so we focus on spaces that can be read safely during loading. The scope is agreed with the superintendent and the master, ordered by priority, and adjusted if the terminal changes the loading programme. The readings go into the class TM layout with wasted areas marked for the yard.
list: Segregated ballast tank gauging on a crude tanker during loading, with tanks prepared on passage to the terminal.
Deck plating and external piping readings on a crude carrier outside the hazardous zone, within the permit.
Forepeak, aft peak and cofferdam gauging on an aframax tanker as part of a pre-docking steel estimate.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard piping gauging on a tanker fitted with an exhaust gas cleaning system.
Pre-purchase condition gauging of a crude tanker lying alongside at the terminal.

logistics: Bergen Airport Flesland is the nearest airport, with connections through Oslo and several European hubs, and the team travels by road to the terminal. The terminal controls entry, and passes and safety inductions are arranged through the vessel's agent in advance. Norway is in the Schengen area, so technicians from India travel on Schengen visas applied for once the call is confirmed; owners with regular Norwegian calls can keep visas valid. Any launch for fjord anchorage work is booked by the agent.
vessels: Offshore supply vessels passing the fjord

faqs.q: Can crude tankers be gauged while loading at Sture?
faqs.a: In part. Ballast tanks, cofferdams, deck plating and external piping outside the hazardous zone can be read during loading, under the terminal's permit and the ship's enclosed-space procedure. Cargo tanks are normally left for drydock. We agree the scope with the master and the terminal before boarding.

faqs.q: What must the crew prepare before the team arrives at Sture?
faqs.a: Ballast tanks chosen for gauging should be pumped out, ventilated and tested gas-free before entry, with lighting and safe access in place. Starting preparation on passage to the terminal gives enough time. We provide the list of tanks in priority order so the crew prepare the most important spaces first.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock near Sture for steel renewal?
faqs.a: No yard at Sture itself. Ships needing steel renewal dock at yards on the Norwegian coast or elsewhere in northern Europe. We use the readings from the terminal to prepare the steel estimate and to agree the renewal list with class before the ship reaches the yard.

faqs.q: Can gauging be done in the fjord while waiting for a berth?
faqs.a: Sometimes a short scope on deck, hatches and air pipes can be done by launch if weather and the terminal's rules allow. The sheltered fjord helps, but cargo operations, hazard zones and boarding arrangements limit what is practical. For a fuller ballast programme, the jetty is the better place.

faqs.q: How is a Sture job organised with a team from India?
faqs.a: The superintendent confirms dates, jetty and scope, we apply for Schengen visas and book flights to Bergen, and the agent arranges terminal passes and safety induction. Loading schedules can shift, so we plan flexibly and keep the scope in priority order, so key readings are taken first.
